title: Asteroid 2026 SZ2 Passed About 9,200 Miles Above Earth, Inside the Orbit of Geostationary Satellites
byline: Sydney Anderson Published: Sep 28 2026, 11:00 AM EDT
excerpt: Asteroid 2026 SZ2 passed about 9,200 miles above Earth on Sept. 20, inside geostationary orbit. Here is how close it came and why it posed no risk.
content:
A small asteroid designated 2026 SZ2 passed about 9,200 miles (14,800 kilometers) above Earth's surface on Sunday, Sept. 20, slipping well inside the high ring where geostationary satellites relay weather data, television, and communications. The object made its closest approach at 21:19 UTC, or 5:19 p.m. EDT, according to The Watchers, which compiled data from NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies and the Minor Planet Center.

Many reports described the pass as 13,100 miles (21,100 kilometers) from Earth. That figure is accurate, but it is measured from the planet's center, the standard used in asteroid close-approach tables. Subtracting Earth's radius of roughly 3,960 miles puts the rock about 9,200 miles above the ground. Geostationary satellites, by comparison, orbit about 22,236 miles above the equator.

The asteroid posed no threat. With an estimated diameter of about 7 to 15 feet (2.1 to 4.6 meters), 2026 SZ2 belongs to a size class that breaks apart high in the atmosphere if it ever enters. The flyby matters less as a hazard than as a real-world check on how quickly survey telescopes catch small objects, and how little notice they sometimes get.

Spotted Hours, Not Days, Before Closest Approach

The University of Arizona's Mount Lemmon Survey in Arizona first observed 2026 SZ2 at about 06:56 UTC on Sept. 20, roughly 14 hours and 23 minutes before closest approach. In other words, it was found before the flyby, but with less than a day of warning.

Over the next 12 hours, observatories in Arizona, Hawaii, China and the United Kingdom added follow-up measurements. The Minor Planet Center logged 27 observations, 26 of which were used to fit an orbit over a one-day arc. Its official object record classifies the rock as an Aten-class near-Earth object, a group whose orbits are, on average, smaller than Earth's and cross it.

NASA's Small-Body Database entry lists the asteroid's orbital solution. The Watchers reported that it passed at a relative speed of 7.99 kilometers per second, or roughly 17,900 miles per hour, with an absolute magnitude of 30.5, a measure of how bright it would appear at a standard distance.

Measuring a Near Miss From Earth's Center

Astronomers often express close approaches in lunar distances, the average gap between Earth and the Moon, about 238,900 miles. By that measure, 2026 SZ2 came within 0.055 lunar distances. Because that figure is measured from Earth's center, the height above the surface is always smaller than the headline number.

Passing inside geostationary altitude does not mean the asteroid came near any satellite. Geostationary spacecraft sit in a narrow belt directly above the equator, while an asteroid's path crosses an enormous volume of space.

The size estimate carries real uncertainty. Diameters for small asteroids are usually inferred from brightness, and a dark rock and a shiny rock of the same brightness can differ in size. That is why the published range spans more than a factor of two. The orbit is also based on a short arc of observations, so its long-term path is less precisely known than that of an asteroid tracked for years.

Close Flybys Are More Common Than Headlines Suggest

The pass was close, but it was not a record. As of Sept. 21, 118 known asteroids had passed within one lunar distance of Earth in 2026, or roughly one every two to three days. 2026 SZ2 tied asteroid 2026 RT34, which passed on Sept. 13, at 0.055 lunar distances. Only two objects came closer this year: 2026 PC6, which passed at 0.053 lunar distances in August, and 2026 JN4, which entered the atmosphere in May.

Small impacts happen too. Earlier this month, asteroid 2026 RW1 struck the atmosphere over the Indian Ocean about seven hours after its discovery, becoming the 13th known asteroid detected before impact. Objects in that size range are routinely destroyed high above the surface.

Danger rises sharply with size. The asteroid that exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013 was roughly 20 meters across, and its airburst shattered windows and injured about 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass. At 2.1 to 4.6 meters, 2026 SZ2 sits far below that threshold.

For context, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has noted that small asteroids of roughly 5 to 10 meters have been seen flying past Earth at distances similar to that of Apophis, a much larger asteroid about 340 meters wide that will pass about 19,000 miles above the surface in April 2029. The rarity lies in large objects coming this close, not small ones. 2026 SZ2 actually passed closer than Apophis will, but it is roughly a hundred times smaller.

Survey Telescopes Keep Watching as Detection Improves

The practical lesson from 2026 SZ2 is about detection, not danger. Survey programs keep finding more small objects as their capabilities improve, which helps explain why close-approach counts are so high. More discoveries do not by themselves mean more asteroids are approaching. They mean telescopes are catching objects that once slipped by unseen.

Readers do not need to take any action. For future flyby claims on social media, the most reliable checks are NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies and the Minor Planet Center, which publish close-approach distances and dates. Be wary of posts that give distances without saying whether they are measured from Earth's center or surface, or that describe small objects as threats.

What remains uncertain is the asteroid's exact size and composition, and how precisely its orbit can be projected decades ahead from a one-day observation arc. Additional archival or future observations could refine those numbers.

Asteroid 2026 SZ2 flew about 9,200 miles above Earth's surface, far closer than geostationary satellites orbit, yet it was small enough to pose no hazard. It was also found before it arrived, a sign that the sky surveys built to catch such objects are working, even if some warnings still come with only hours to spare.

What Readers Want to Know

How close did asteroid 2026 SZ2 come to Earth?

It passed about 13,100 miles (21,100 kilometers) from Earth's center, or roughly 9,200 miles (14,800 kilometers) above the surface, at 5:19 p.m. EDT on Sept. 20, 2026.

Why do some reports say 13,100 miles and others 9,200 miles?

Close-approach tables measure distance from Earth's center. Subtracting Earth's radius gives the approximate height above the surface.

Was 2026 SZ2 dangerous?

No. At an estimated 7 to 15 feet across, it would have broken apart high in the atmosphere had it entered, and it was never on a collision course.

Was the asteroid detected before or after it passed Earth?

Before. The Mount Lemmon Survey in Arizona spotted it about 14 hours and 23 minutes before closest approach.

How often do asteroids pass this close?

Asteroids passing within one lunar distance are common. As of Sept. 21, 118 had been logged in 2026, though only a few came as close as 2026 SZ2.

Where can I check official asteroid flyby data?

NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies and the Minor Planet Center publish close-approach distances, dates, and orbital data for known asteroids.
